title: When you miss a day
hook: the tradition expects stumbling; you simply begin again
tomorrow: a sage warned a fixed prayer can go dead. so do you change it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Onkelos at the door: the words hang at the exit so they go out with you. Carry the words out. But some days, you don't carry anything out at all.
screen: `CARRY THE WORDS OUT.` → `AND THE DAYS YOU DON'T?`

segments.voice: Streak counters are ruthless. Miss one morning and the number you were proud of drops back to zero, and quitting starts to look reasonable. The Torah has a much bigger miss. Moses comes down the mountain, sees the golden calf, and smashes the first tablets. Later he carves a new pair, and God writes the same words again. So far, a clean restart. But the Talmud adds a strange detail: the broken pieces were kept too. Why keep the broken pieces?
screen: `MISS ONE MORNING: BACK TO ZERO.` → `THE FIRST TABLETS, SMASHED.` → `WHY KEEP THE PIECES?`

segments.voice: Both went into the Ark, the Talmud says: the whole tablets and the broken ones, side by side, in the Ark itself. And it draws its own lesson from that, about people. Honor an elder who has forgotten his learning through no fault of his own, because the broken tablets also rest in the Ark. Brokenness doesn't get thrown out. It gets carried, with honor. Proverbs puts the same idea in one line: a righteous person falls seven times, and rises up again. Read it slowly. Falling is inside the sentence. Seven times, even. The verse doesn't define the righteous as the ones who never fall; it defines them as the ones who get up. So when you miss a day, the tradition isn't surprised, and it doesn't send you back to zero. The missed days go into the box with the good ones, and you begin again from where you are, not from the start. Something to tell a friend tonight: in the Ark, the broken tablets sat right next to the whole ones.
screen: `WHOLE AND BROKEN, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `HONOR THE ONE WHO FORGOT.` · `FALLS SEVEN TIMES, AND RISES.` · `NO RESET TO ZERO.` · then, large: `BEGIN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: If you're able, sit all the way down, and let yourself settle as if you'd just stumbled. Then stand slowly, feeling your feet take your weight again. Sit, and rise, once or twice more, without hurrying: the falling is in the sentence, and so is the rising.
When you miss a day: the tradition expects it. The broken days are kept, not erased, and you begin again from where you stand.
screen: `WHEN YOU MISS A DAY — today's word`.

segments.voice: For the road: begin again. The broken days ride along in the Ark; they don't send you back to zero.

screen: `DAY 1661 COUNTS.` → `A RULE OF LIFE · 14 OF 15.` → `TOMORROW: A FIXED PRAYER CAN GO DEAD. CHANGE IT?`

howItsDone: Jewish teaching on teshuvah, returning, expects lapses: someone who misses prayers, study or a practice is taught to pick it up again at the next opportunity rather than abandon it; Elul and the High Holy Days give the whole community a set time to begin again.

notes: Berakhot 8b: Rabbi Joshua ben Levi (honor an elder who forgot his learning 'through no fault of his own' — the Talmud says due to circumstances beyond his control), tied to the tablets and the broken tablets in the Ark. Confirm wording.
